rv.q: Any qualms theater-lovers might have about this being a premature revival will vanish like frost in strong sunlight.
It has awakened "Spring Awakening."
It ranks among the most emotionally charged renderings of a musical to come to Broadway in the past decade, one that all who love the genre should rush to see.
Deaf West awakens something new in the show, which is not so much a revival as it is a reinvention.

Occasionally — and Theatre’s production of Spring Awakening is a superb example — something latent in the material meets the mood of the time to make a revival not just a necessity but a great pleasure.
This moving Broadway revival, then, seals a pact with an audience in a gentler manner than the more scaldingly assertive original production, which won eight Tony Awards, including best musical.
There is also considerable power when a couple of the deaf actors, unable to make themselves understood to their parents, shout in their own unpracticed anguished voices
The results are moving and both visually and musically impressive, if ultimately a bit repetitious.
But while the intent merits applause, the execution is not sufficiently fresh or Broadway-caliber to justify the swift return.
Admiring this revival’s feat is one thing. Feeling for it — now, that’s something else.
For all of the valid reservations one can have about this experiment, there’s still beauty to admire, if you’re willing to hear.
The lighting may be dappled but Spring Awakening is brilliant.
It's a darkly sumptuous, ultimately uplifting feast for the ears and eyes.
This revival is that rare reimagining that furthers the themes of the original work, rather than plastering over them with an auteur's vision.

Although it’s hard to shake off memories of the brilliant original production (which had a cast including Jonathan Groff, Lea Michele, John Gallagher Jr. and Skylar Astin), Arden’s revival is visually stunning, emotionally poignant and thoroughly exciting in its own right.
This cast of mostly unknowns couldn't be better

For those who found the original production goofy or even alienating, the company’s introduction of American Sign Language grants the show more heft and sincerity, and in turn a new level of intimacy.
Lines and lyrics look as poetic and provocative as they sound.
Michael Arden's meticulous direction adds the poetry and emotion that gives this version its resonance.
The addition of sign language encourages a closer look at “Spring Awakening.”
And certainly by the end of act two, you’ll wonder why all actors in all musicals don’t use American Sign Language to convey what they’re singing.
'Spring Awakening' is just not a good musical...A smarmy evening that, as writing, satisfies on no theatrical level
The staging lacks flow, as do the book and lyrics.
It is undoubtedly one of the most unforgettable theatrical experiences I've seen.
It's quite extraordinary when you can improve upon perfection. Dare I say, it's better than the original.
This show is a must see! A perfect night at the theater.
This production is nuanced and singular.
A company featuring deaf actors is bringing the sound of music to Broadway in a revival even more thrilling than its original production
With this revival, everything made sense. Every line, every beat was explored to its full potential and it was executed perfectly.
Do yourself a favor and see this before it closes in January.
This new production is a wildly impactful and visceral production that goes straight to the heart and doesn't let go.

Aided by a tight band of strings and drums, by inspired and precise lighting, and by smartly repressed costuming and somber scenic design with a gorgeous surprise at the end, the brilliant direction and choreography turn 'Spring Awakening,' already a fine if unusual musical, into something really special and new.

That such a show should be so joyful and so beautiful — from the evocative lighting of Ben Stanton to the hand ballet of sign language by the entire cast — is itself a sign: Deaf West has done it right.
'Spring Awakening' is a refreshing challenge to the rigid Broadway template.
Arden proves here that a dark musical can be a very stirring—and soulful--experience.
This is about as cohesive and powerful a production of this show as I'm ever likely to see.
Even with a few missteps though, this production is worth every second of your time, if just to take in the glorious songs.
Let me assure you that Deaf West's production is well worth seeing
'Spring Awakening' 2015 is quite moving and feels even more organic than the in-your-face, bold original.
At times the show feels like there is too much going on; this makes for an experience that is often more rewarding on an intellectual, rather than an emotional level.
Wedekind's play is fully realized in the dynamic staging, but there's also a cool grayness that creates a sense of distance
Michael Arden's direction and vision are wonderfully executed.
Individual performances and breakthrough moments that marry signing and storytelling make for emotional impact, one that's felt in fits and starts rather than as major payoff.
I wasn't really moved by the production itself
